section.title: Emulator options
section.p: The postrisc is a console application for all basic tasks. Uses standard streams for input/output that need to be redirected from file or to file. It is called with different keys from the command line (table below).

section.title: LLVM backend intro
section.p: The llvm tablegen information about the instructions encoding, the format of machine instructions, operation codes, etc, is also generated automatically. See it in PostriscInstrEncoding.td in LLVM compiler backend.

section.title: LLVM backend limitations
section.p: Nullification - it works!
Pre/post update addressing is not worked.
Loop instructions aren't used in compiler.
Currently, only static PIE executables are supported by compiler and emulator.

section.title: Code density comparison
section.p: Here are results for SQLite 3.33.0 compiled with Clang 10.0.1 on FreeBSD 12.1 with -Os for various architectures:

where a32 is ARMv7-A in ARM mode, t32 is the same in thumb mode and a64 is ARMv8-A. The rest are self explanatory. The clear winner is ARM Thumb, but RISC-V does well indeed (with compressed instructions, without it's rather meh) It's the most space efficient 64 bit ISA for sure. i686 does a little worse (still the third most compact after RV32gc and T32) and the classic RISC instruction sets are just terrible. The clear loser is Z/Architecture (S390x).

The SQLite 3.33.0 sqlite-chromium-version-3.33.0, (probably same sources), compiled with Clang 24.0.0git on Linux. The results for are without (not implemented yet in the compiler) using the base pre-update addressing mode and the loop instructions, which may improve code density a bit. Auto-vectorization is completely disabled for all architectures because doesn't supported for yet.
The Oz optimization: maximal code compression
The Os optimization
The O2 optimization

The main factor for code density is the possibility of returning inside the middle of an instruction bundle (dense vs aligned) and the using of nullification (null). In common, code density for is more or less similar to MIPS, PowerPC, Sparc, LoongArch, S390, and RISC-V (without compression) or only slightly worse. This is surprising taking into account 128 registers, bundles, nops, etc. The clear loser is MIPS.

section.title: DOOM port
section.p: port for Doom-1: github.com/bdpx/postrisc_doom. Uses the MUSL standard library (as a static lib). Doom generic interface is implemented as additional system calls.

The emulator log doom-log.html with static/dynamic instruction statistic for Doom Shareware demo scene autoplay. First 3 demoscenes, limited to 10 billion instructions. User time: 123.152 seconds. System time: 62.927 seconds. Frames: 12886. Iinstructions per frame: 776036 (up to 8-bit indexed image not counting emulator scaling/mapping). Instructions per pixel: 12.125. Frames per second: 69.249.

section.title: Todo
section.p: A set of tools for working with (assembler, disassembler, emulator is implemented) is incomplete. Further directions for improvement (the number in brackets like [2] characterizes the comparative complexity of the tasks):

ol.li: Development of a macroprocessor for the assembler [3].
Refactoring the formula calculation unit to introduce strict control over the use of object names in formulas (according to sections and segments of the program and the relocation types) [2].
Development of the object file format for a virtual processor compatible with the ELF standard, processing assembler for ELF [2].
Development of separate compilation tools, support for relocation records according to the ELF standard (Executable and Linkable Format) in assembler and the development of the linker [2].
Development of a visual debugger for the emulator [2].
Development of a text editor with syntax highlighting of the assembler virtual processor [2].
Adding new hardware tools to the virtual processor architecture and its emulator: cache management, virtual memory and translation buffer [2].

Development of a simulator (cycle-accurate emulator) of the possible hardware implementation of a virtual processor, with the simulation of hardware such as multi-level instruction/data caches, translation buffers, branch prediction cache, return prediction stack, and other modern hardware. [5]
